stem: Rufaro Garments is a fictional clothing factory in Bulawayo with 40 machinists. Its maximum capacity is 12,000 shirts a month. Last month it made 9,000 shirts and its labour cost was US\$27,000. The owner wants to raise productivity and make better use of the factory.

parts.label: (i)
parts.stem: capacity utilisation, to one decimal place;

parts.label: (ii)
parts.stem: spare capacity, in shirts a month.

parts.label: (i)
parts.stem: labour productivity, in shirts per machinist;

parts.label: (ii)
parts.stem: the labour cost of each shirt.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Outline two ways in which Rufaro Garments could increase labour productivity.

points.description: Train the machinists in faster and more accurate methods
Application: skilled machinists sew more shirts in the same time with fewer faults
Buy better sewing machines or improve the layout of the work
Application: new machines or a better layout reduce the time each shirt takes

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The factory could train the machinists in faster and more accurate methods, so each sews more shirts in the same time with fewer faults. It could also buy better sewing machines or improve the layout of the work, which reduces the time each shirt takes.

parts.explanation: Two ways, each outlined with a result.

explanation: Utilisation 75.0%, spare capacity 3,000 shirts, productivity 225 shirts per machinist and labour cost US\$3.00 a shirt.
hints: Labour productivity = output ÷ number of employees.

stem: Tafara Bakery is a fictional business in Mutare that makes 5,000 cakes a month. Direct costs are US\$1.80 a cake and monthly overheads are US\$3,000, shared equally between the cakes. The owner sets the price by adding a mark-up of 40% to the full cost of a cake. A rival bakery has just started selling similar cakes at US\$3.

parts.label: (i)
parts.stem: the full cost of a cake;
parts.explanation: Overheads per cake = 3,000 ÷ 5,000 = 0.60. Full cost = 1.80 + 0.60 = US\$2.40.
parts.workedSolution: 1. Overheads per cake = 3,000 ÷ 5,000 = 0.60. Full cost = 1.80 + 0.60 = US\$2.40.

parts.label: (ii)
parts.stem: the selling price of a cake.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Match each pricing strategy to its description.

right.content: A low price at launch to win market share
A high price at launch to earn a large profit on each unit

parts.explanation: Penetration is low-price entry; skimming is high-price entry.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Discuss whether Tafara Bakery should reduce its price to match the rival's price of US\$3.00.

points.description: At US\$3.36 the profit is US\$0.96 a cake, or US\$4,800 a month on 5,000 cakes
At US\$3.00 the profit falls to US\$0.60 a cake, or US\$3,000 a month, if sales stay the same
A lower price may keep customers who would otherwise buy from the rival
Judgement with a condition, for example: match the price only if sales would otherwise fall by more than a third

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: At US\$3.36 each cake earns US\$0.96, or US\$4,800 a month, but at US\$3.00 the profit falls to US\$0.60 a cake, or US\$3,000 a month, if sales stay the same. A lower price may keep customers who would otherwise buy from the rival. The bakery should match the price only if it would otherwise lose more than about a third of its sales.

parts.explanation: Profit comparison and a conditional judgement.
hints: Compare the monthly profit at each price.

explanation: Full cost US\$2.40 and price US\$3.36; matching US\$3.00 cuts profit per cake from US\$0.96 to US\$0.60.
hints: Share the overheads over the cakes to find the full cost.

stem: Zuva Hardware is a fictional shop in Gweru that sells 7,200 bags of cement a year. It costs US\$50 to place an order and US\$2 to hold one bag in stock for a year. The manager uses the economic order quantity (EOQ = √(2DS ÷ H), where D is yearly demand, S the cost of placing an order and H the yearly holding cost of one bag).

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: At the economic order quantity, calculate:

parts.label: (i)
parts.stem: the number of orders placed in a year;

parts.label: (ii)
parts.stem: the total yearly cost of ordering and holding stock.
parts.explanation: Ordering cost = 12 × 50 = 600. Holding cost = (600 ÷ 2) × 2 = 600. Total = US\$1,200.
parts.workedSolution: 1. Ordering cost = 12 × 50 = 600. Holding cost = (600 ÷ 2) × 2 = 600. Total = US\$1,200.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Explain two limitations of using the economic order quantity.

points.description: It assumes that demand is constant, but cement sales vary with the season
Application: in the building season demand could be much higher than 7,200 a year divided evenly
It ignores discounts for bulk orders and delays in delivery
Application: a supplier may offer a lower price for larger orders, or deliver late, so a buffer may be needed

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The model assumes that demand is constant, but cement sales vary with the building season, so the best order size changes through the year. It also ignores discounts for bulk orders and delays in delivery, so a supplier's discount or a late lorry may make a different order size or a buffer stock better.

parts.explanation: Two limitations, each applied to cement.
hints: Think about the assumptions of the model.

explanation: EOQ 600 bags, 12 orders a year and total cost US\$1,200 (ordering US\$600 plus holding US\$600).
hints: At the EOQ the ordering cost equals the holding cost.
